entries.4ca8f74532ff3a6517c120e8504800a90aff0bdb: <div sID="gen12161" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="94" osisID="Ps.94" sID="Ps.94"/> <div eID="gen12161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12162" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12163" type="x-p"/> This psalm was penned when the church of God was under hatches, oppressed and persecuted; and it is an appeal to God, as the judge of heaven and earth, and an address to him, to appear for his people against his and their enemies. Two things this psalm speaks:—I. Conviction and terror to the persecutors (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.1-Ps.94.11">ver. 1-11</reference>), showing them their danger and folly, and arguing with them. II. Comfort and peace to the persecuted (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.12-Ps.94.23">ver. 12-23</reference>), assuring them, both from God's promise and from the psalmist's own experience, that their troubles would end well, and God would, in due time, appear to their joy and the confusion of those who set themselves against them. In singing this psalm we must look abroad upon the pride of oppressors with a holy indignation, and the tears of the oppressed with a holy compassion; but, at the same time, look upwards to the righteous Judge with an entire satisfaction, and look forward, to the end of all these things, with a pleasing hope.
entries.7b796616de9dc0ee4584494429766cd6ae039836: <div eID="gen12163" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12162" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Appeal to God against Persecutors; The Folly of Atheists and Oppressors.</title> <div sID="gen12164" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, show thyself. <hi type="super">2</hi> Lift up thyself, thou judge of the earth: render a reward to the proud. <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked triumph? <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="italic">How long</hi> shall they utter <hi type="italic">and</hi> speak hard things? <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the workers of iniquity boast themselves? <hi type="super">5</hi> They break in pieces thy people, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and afflict thine heritage. <hi type="super">6</hi> They slay the widow and the stranger, and murder the fatherless. <hi type="super">7</hi> Yet they say, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> Understand, ye brutish among the people: and <hi type="italic">ye</hi> fools, when will ye be wise? <hi type="super">9</hi> He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see? <hi type="super">10</hi> He that chastiseth the heathen, shall not he correct? he that teacheth man knowledge, <hi type="italic">shall not he know?</hi> 11 The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> knoweth the thoughts of man, that they <hi type="italic">are</hi> vanity. <div eID="gen12164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12165" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen12165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12166" type="x-p"/> I. A solemn appeal to God against the cruel oppressors of his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.1-Ps.94.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. This speaks terror enough to them, that they have the prayers of God's people against them, who cry day and night to him to avenge them of their adversaries; and shall he not avenge them speedily? <reference osisRef="Luke.18.3">Luke xviii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.7">7</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen12166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12167" type="x-p"/> 1. The titles they give to God for the encouraging of their faith in this appeal: <hi type="italic">O God! to whom vengeance belongeth;</hi> and <hi type="italic">thou Judge of the earth.</hi> We may with boldness appeal to him; for, (1.) He is judge, supreme judge, judge alone, from whom every man's judgment proceeds. He that gives law gives sentence upon every man according to his works, by the rule of that law. He has prepared his throne for judgment. He has indeed appointed magistrates to be avengers under him (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 4</reference>), but he is the avenger in chief, to whom even magistrates themselves are accountable; his throne is the last refuge (the <hi type="italic">dernier ressort,</hi> as the law speaks) of oppressed innocency. He is universal judge, not of this city or country only, but <hi type="italic">judge of the earth,</hi> of the whole earth: none are exempt from his jurisdiction; nor can it be alleged against an appeal to him in any court that it is <hi type="italic">coram non judice—before a person not judicially qualified.</hi> (2.) He is just. As he has authority to avenge wrong, so it is his nature, and property, and honour. This also is implied in the title here given to him and repeated with such an emphasis, <hi type="italic">O God! to whom vengeance belongs,</hi> who wilt not suffer might always to prevail against right. This is a good reason why we must not avenge ourselves, because God has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine;</hi> and it is daring presumption to usurp his prerogative and step into his throne, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.19">Rom. xii. 19</reference>. Let this alarm those who do wrong, whether with a close hand, so as not to be discovered, or with a high hand, so as not to be controlled, There is a God to whom vengeance belongs, who will certainly call them to an account; and let it encourage those who suffer wrong to bear it with silence, committing themselves to him who judges righteously. <div eID="gen12167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12168" type="x-p"/> 2. What it is they ask of God. (1.) That he would <hi type="italic">glorify himself,</hi> and get honour to his own name. Wicked persecutors thought God had withdrawn and had forsaken the earth. "Lord," say they, "show thyself; make them know that thou art and that thou art ready to <hi type="italic">show thyself strong on the behalf of those whose hearts are upright with thee.</hi>" The enemies thought God was conquered because his people were. "Lord," say they, "<hi type="italic">lift up thyself, be thou exalted in thy own strength.</hi> Lift up thyself, to be seen, to be feared; and suffer not thy name to be trampled upon and run down." (2.) That he would mortify the oppressors: <hi type="italic">Render a reward to the proud;</hi> that is, "Reckon with them for all their insolence, and the injuries they have done to thy people." These prayers are prophecies, which speak terror to all the sons of violence. The righteous God will deal with them according to their merits. <div eID="gen12168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12169" type="x-p"/> II. A humble complaint to God of the pride and cruelty of the oppressors, and an expostulation with him concerning it, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.3-Ps.94.6">v. 3-6</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen12169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12170" type="x-p"/> 1. The character of the enemies they complain against. They are wicked; they are <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity;</hi> they are bad, very bad, themselves, and therefore they hate and persecute those whose goodness shames and condemns them. Those are wicked indeed, and <hi type="italic">workers of the worst iniquity,</hi> lost to all honour and virtue, who are cruel to the innocent and hate the righteous. <div eID="gen12170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12171" type="x-p"/> 2. Their haughty barbarous carriage which they complain of. (1.) They are insolent, and take a pleasure in magnifying themselves. They talk high and talk big; they triumph; they speak loud things; they boast themselves, as if their tongues were their own and their hands too, and they were accountable to none for what they say or do, and as if the day were their own, and they doubted not but to carry the cause against God and religion. Those that speak highly of themselves, that triumph and boast, are apt to speak hardly of others; but there will come a day of reckoning for all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against God, his truths, and ways, and people, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. (2.) They are impious, and take a pleasure in running down God's people because they are his (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">They break in pieces thy people, O Lord!</hi> break their assemblies, their estates, their families, their persons, in pieces, and do all they can to afflict thy heritage, to grieve them, to crush them, to run them down, to root them out." God's people are his heritage; there are those that, for his sake, hate them, and seek their ruin. This is a very good plea with God, in our intercessions for the church: "Lord, it is thine; thou hast a property in it. It is thy heritage; thou hast a pleasure in it, and out of it the rent of thy glory in this world issues. And wilt thou suffer these wicked men to trample upon it thus?" (3.) They are inhuman, and take a pleasure in wronging those that are least able to help themselves (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.6">v. 6</reference>); they not only oppress and impoverish, but <hi type="italic">they slay the widow and the stranger;</hi> not only neglect the fatherless, and make a prey of them, but murder them, because they are weak and exposed, and sometimes lie at their mercy. Those whom they should protect from injury they are most injurious to, perhaps because God has taken them into his particular care. Who would think it possible that any of the children of men should be thus barbarous? <div eID="gen12171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12172" type="x-p"/> 3. A modest pleading with God concerning the continuance of the persecution: "Lord, <hi type="italic">how long</hi> shall they do thus?" And again, <hi type="italic">How long?</hi> When shall this wickedness of the wicked come to an end? <div eID="gen12172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12173" type="x-p"/> III. A charge of atheism exhibited against the persecutors, and an expostulation with them upon that charge. <div eID="gen12173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12174" type="x-p"/> 1. Their atheistical thoughts are here discovered (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet they say, The Lord shall not see.</hi> Though the cry of their wickedness is very great and loud, though they rebel against the light of nature and the dictates of their own consciences, yet they have the confidence to say, "<hi type="italic">The Lord shall not see;</hi> he will not only wink at small faults, but shut his eyes at great ones too." Or they think they have managed it so artfully, under colour of justice and religion perhaps, that it will not be adjudged murder. "The God of Jacob, though his people pretend to have such an interest in him, does not regard it either as against justice or as against his own people; he will never call us to an account for it." Thus they deny God's government of the world, banter his covenant with his people, and set the judgment to come at defiance. <div eID="gen12174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12175" type="x-p"/> 2. They are here convicted of folly and absurdity. He that says either that Jehovah the living God shall not see or that the God of Jacob shall not regard the injuries done to his people, <hi type="italic">Nabal</hi> is his name and folly is with him; and yet here he is fairly reasoned with, for his conviction and conversion, to prevent his confusion (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Understand, you brutish among the people,</hi> and let reason guide you." Note, The atheistical, though they set up for wits, and philosophers, and politicians, yet are really the <hi type="italic">brutish among the people;</hi> if they would but understand, they would believe. God, by the prophet, speaks as if he thought the time long till men would be men, and show themselves so by understanding and considering: "<hi type="italic">You fools, when will you be wise,</hi> so wise as to know that God sees and regards all you say and do, and to speak and act accordingly, as those that must give account?" Note, None are so bad but means are to be used for the reclaiming and reforming of them, none so brutish, so foolish, but it should be tried whether they may not yet be made wise; while there is life there is hope. To prove the folly of those that question God's omniscience and justice the psalmist argues, <div eID="gen12175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12176" type="x-p"/> (1.) From the works of creation (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">v. 9</reference>), the formation of human bodies, which as it proves that there is a God, proves also that God has infinitely and transcendently in himself all those perfections that are in any creature. <hi type="italic">He that planted the ear</hi> (and it is planted in the head, as a tree in the ground) <hi type="italic">shall he not hear?</hi> No doubt he shall, more and better than we can. <hi type="italic">He that formed the eye</hi> (and how curiously it is formed above any part of the body anatomists know and let us know by their dissections) <hi type="italic">shall he not see?</hi> Could he give, would he give, that perfection to a creature which he has not in himself? Note, [1.] The powers of nature are all derived from the God of nature. See <reference osisRef="Exod.4.11">Exod. iv. 11</reference>. [2.] By the knowledge of ourselves we may be led a great way towards the knowledge of God—if by the knowledge of our own bodies, and the organs of sense, so as to conclude that if we can see and hear much more can God, then certainly by the knowledge of our own souls and their noble faculties. The gods of the heathen had eyes and saw not, ears and heard not; our God has no eyes nor ears, as we have, and yet we must conclude he both sees and hears, because we have our sight and hearing from him, and are accountable to him for our use of them. <div eID="gen12176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12177" type="x-p"/> (2.) From the works of providence (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that chastises the heathen</hi> for their polytheism and idolatry, <hi type="italic">shall not he</hi> much more <hi type="italic">correct</hi> his own people for their atheism and profaneness? He that chastises the children of men for oppressing and wronging one another, shall not he correct those that profess to be his own children, and call themselves so, and yet persecute those that are really so? Shall not we be under his correction, under whose government the whole world is? Does he regard as King of nations, and shall he not much more regard as the God of Jacob? Dr. Hammond gives another very probably sense of this: "<hi type="italic">He that instructs the nations</hi> (that is, gives them his law), <hi type="italic">shall not he correct,</hi> that is, shall not he judge them according to that law, and call them to an account for their violations of it? In vain was the law given if there will not be a judgment upon it." And it is true that the same word signifies to chastise and to instruct, because chastisement is intended for instruction and instruction should go along with chastisement. <div eID="gen12177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12178" type="x-p"/> (3.) From the works of grace: <hi type="italic">He that teaches man knowledge, shall he not know?</hi> He not only, as the God of nature, has given the light of reason, but, as the God of grace, has given the light of revelation, has shown man what is true wisdom and understanding; and he that does this, shall he not know? <reference osisRef="Job.28.23">Job xxviii. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">28</reference>. The flowing of the streams is a certain sign of the fulness of the fountain. If all knowledge is from God, no doubt all knowledge is in God. From this general doctrine of God's omniscience, the psalmist not only confutes the atheists, who said, "<hi type="italic">The Lord shall not see</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">v. 7</reference>), he will not take cognizance of what we do;" but awakens us all to consider that God will take cognizance even of what we think (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are vanity.</hi> [1.] He knows those thoughts in particular, concerning God's conniving at the wickedness of the wicked, and knows them to be vain, and laughs at the folly of those who by such fond conceits buoy themselves up in sin. [2.] He knows all the thoughts of the children of men, and knows them to be, for the most part, vain, that the imaginations of the thoughts of men's hearts are evil, only evil, and that continually. Even in good thoughts there is a fickleness and inconstancy which may well be called <hi type="italic">vanity.</hi> It concerns us to keep a strict guard upon our thoughts, because God takes particular notice of them. Thoughts are words to God, and vain thoughts are provocations.
entries.1c8848e45f8922bb11aefced467163b10802a738: <div eID="gen12178" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Comfort to Suffering Saints; God the Defence of His People.</title> <div sID="gen12179" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man whom thou chastenest, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and teachest him out of thy law; <hi type="super">13</hi> That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity, until the pit be digged for the wicked. <hi type="super">14</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance. <hi type="super">15</hi> But judgment shall return unto righteousness: and all the upright in heart shall follow it. <hi type="super">16</hi> Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? <hi type="italic">or</hi> who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity? <hi type="super">17</hi> Unless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">had been</hi> my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence. <hi type="super">18</hi> When I said, My foot slippeth; thy mercy, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , held me up. <hi type="super">19</hi> In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul. <hi type="super">20</hi> Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law? <hi type="super">21</hi> They gather themselves together against the soul of the righteous, and condemn the innocent blood. <hi type="super">22</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is my defence; and my God <hi type="italic">is</hi> the rock of my refuge. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness; <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God shall cut them off. <div eID="gen12179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12180" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having denounced tribulation to those that trouble God's people, here assures those that are troubled of rest. See <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6-2Thess.1.7">2 Thess. i. 6, 7</reference>. He speaks comfort to suffering saints from God's promises and his own experience. <div eID="gen12180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12181" type="x-p"/> I. From God's promises, which are such as not only save them from being miserable, but secure a happiness to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest.</hi> Here he looks above the instruments of trouble, and eyes the hand of God, which gives it another name and puts quite another color upon it. The enemies break in pieces God's people (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.5">v. 5</reference>); they aim at no less; but the truth of the matter is that God by them chastens his people, as the father the son in whom he delights, and the persecutors are only the rod he makes use of. <hi type="italic">Howbeit they mean not so, neither doth their heart think so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 5-7</reference>. Now it is here promised, <div eID="gen12181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12182" type="x-p"/> 1. That God's people shall get good by their sufferings. When he chastens them he will teach them, and blessed is the man who is thus taken under a divine discipline, for <hi type="italic">none teaches like God.</hi> Note, (1.) The afflictions of the saints are fatherly chastenings, designed for their instruction, reformation, and improvement. (2.) When the teachings of the word and Spirit go along with the rebukes of Providence they then both manifest men to be blessed and help to make them so; for then they are marks of adoption and means of sanctification. When we are chastened we must pray to be taught, and look into the law as the best expositor of Providence. It is not the chastening itself that does good, but the teaching that goes along with it and is the exposition of it. <div eID="gen12182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12183" type="x-p"/> 2. That they shall see through their sufferings (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity.</hi> Note, (1.) There is a rest remaining for the people of God after the days of their adversity, which, though they may be many and long, shall be numbered and finished in due time, and shall not last always. He that sends the trouble will send the rest, that he may comfort them according to the time that he has afflicted them. (2.) God <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> teaches his people by their troubles, that he may prepare them for deliverance, and so give them rest from their troubles, that, being reformed, they may be relieved, and that the affliction, having done its work, may be removed. <div eID="gen12183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12184" type="x-p"/> 3. That they shall see the ruin of those that are the instruments of their sufferings, which is the matter of a promise, not as gratifying any passion of theirs, but as redounding to the glory of God: <hi type="italic">Until the pit is digged</hi> (or rather while the pit is digging) <hi type="italic">for the wicked,</hi> God is ordering peace for them at the same time that he is ordaining his arrows against the persecutors. <div eID="gen12184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12185" type="x-p"/> 4. That, though they may be cast down, yet certainly they shall not be cast off, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.14">v. 14</reference>. Let God's suffering people assure themselves of this, that, whatever their friends do, God will not cast them off, nor throw them out of his covenant or out of his care; he will not forsake them, because they are his inheritance, which he will not quit his title to nor suffer himself to be disseised of. St. Paul comforted himself with this, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen12185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12186" type="x-p"/> 5. That, bad as things are, they shall mend, and, though they are now out of course, yet they shall return to their due and ancient channel (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judgment shall return unto righteousness;</hi> the seeming disorders of Providence (for real ones there never were) shall be rectified. God's judgment, that is, his government, looks sometimes as if it were at a distance from righteousness, while the wicked prosper, and the best men meet with the worst usage; but it shall return to righteousness again, either in this world or at the furthest in the judgment of the great day, which will set all to-rights. Then <hi type="italic">all the upright in heart shall be after it;</hi> they shall follow it with their praises, and with entire satisfaction; they shall return to a prosperous and flourishing condition, and shine forth out of obscurity; they shall accommodate themselves to the dispensations of divine Providence, and with suitable affections attend all its motions. <hi type="italic">They shall walk after the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.10">Hos. xi. 10</reference>. Dr. Hammond thinks this was most eminently fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem first, and afterwards of heathen Rome, the crucifiers of Christ and persecutors of Christians, and the rest which the churches had thereby. <hi type="italic">Then judgment returned even to righteousness,</hi> to mercy and goodness, and favour to God's people, who then were as much countenanced as before they had been trampled on. <div eID="gen12186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12187" type="x-p"/> II. From his own experiences and observations. <div eID="gen12187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12188" type="x-p"/> 1. He and his friends had been oppressed by cruel and imperious men, that had power in their hands and abused it by abusing all good people with it. They were themselves <hi type="italic">evil-doers</hi> and <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">v. 16</reference>); they abandoned themselves to all manner of impiety and immorality, and then their throne was a <hi type="italic">throne of iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.94.20">v. 20</reference>. Their dignity served to put a reputation upon sin, and their authority was employed to support it, and to bring about their wicked designs. It is a pity that ever a throne, which should be a terror to evil-doers and a protection and praise to those that do well, should be the seat and shelter of iniquity. That is a throne of iniquity which by the policy of its council <hi type="italic">frames mischief,</hi> and by its sovereignty enacts it and turns it into a law. Iniquity is daring enough even when human laws are against it, which often prove too weak to give an effectual check to it; but how insolent, how mischievous, is it when it is backed by a law! Iniquity is not the better, but much the worse, for being enacted by law; nor will it excuse those that practise it to say that they did but do as they were bidden. These workers of iniquity, having <hi type="italic">framed mischief by a law, take care to see the law executed;</hi> for <hi type="italic">they gather themselves together against the soul of the righteous,</hi> who dare not <hi type="italic">keep the statutes of Omri</hi> nor <hi type="italic">the law of the house of Ahab;</hi> and they <hi type="italic">condemn the innocent blood</hi> for violating their decrees. See an instance in Daniel's enemies; they <hi type="italic">framed mischief by a law</hi> when the obtained an impious edict against prayer (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">Dan. vi. 7</reference>), and, when Daniel would not obey it, they <hi type="italic">assembled together against</hi> him (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">v. 11</reference>) and <hi type="italic">condemned his innocent blood</hi> to the lions. The best benefactors of mankind have often been thus treated, under colour of law and justice, as the worst of malefactors. <div eID="gen12188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12189" type="x-p"/> 2. The oppression they were under bore very hard upon them, and oppressed their spirits too. Let not suffering saints despair, though, when they are persecuted, they find themselves perplexed and cast down; it was so with the psalmist here: His <hi type="italic">soul had almost dwelt in silence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.17">v. 17</reference>); he was at his wits' end, and knew not what to say or do; he was, in his own apprehensions, at his life's end, ready to drop into the grave, that land of silence. St. Paul, in a like case, <hi type="italic">received a sentence of death within himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8-2Cor.1.9">2 Cor. i. 8, 9</reference>. He said, "<hi type="italic">My foot slippeth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.18">v. 18</reference>); I am going irretrievably; there is no remedy; I must <hi type="italic">fall.</hi> I <hi type="italic">shall one day perish by the hand of Saul.</hi> My hope fails me; I do not find such firm footing for my faith as I have sometimes found." <reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Ps. lxxiii. 2</reference>. He had a multitude of perplexed entangled thoughts within him concerning the case he was in and the construction to be made of it, and concerning the course he should take and what was likely to be the issue of it. <div eID="gen12189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12190" type="x-p"/> 3. In this distress they sought for help, and succour, and some relief. (1.) They looked about for it and were disappointed (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Who will rise up for me against the evil-doers?</hi> Have I any friend who, in love to me, will appear for me? Has justice any friend who, in a pious indignation at unrighteousness, will plead my injured cause?" He looked, but there was none to save, there was none to uphold. Note, When on the side of the oppressors there is power it is no marvel if the oppressed have no comforter, none that dare own them, or speak a good word for them, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Eccl. iv. 1</reference>. When St. Paul was brought before Nero's throne of iniquity <hi type="italic">no man stood by him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2 Tim. iv. 16</reference>. (2.) They looked up for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.20">v. 20</reference>. They humbly expostulate with God: "Lord, <hi type="italic">shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee?</hi> Wilt thou countenance and support these tyrants in their wickedness? We know thou wilt not." A throne has fellowship with God when it is a throne of justice and answers the end of the erecting of it; for by him kings reign, and when they reign for him their judgments are his, and he owns them as his ministers, and whoever resist them, or rise up against them, shall receive to themselves damnation; but, when it becomes a <hi type="italic">throne of iniquity,</hi> it has no longer fellowship with God. Far be it from the just and holy God that he should be the patron of unrighteousness, even in princes and those that sit in thrones, yea, though they be the <hi type="italic">thrones of the house of David.</hi> <div eID="gen12190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12191" type="x-p"/> 4. They found succour and relief in God, and in him only. When other friends failed, in him they had a faithful and powerful friend; and it is recommended to all God's suffering saints to trust in him. (1.) God helps at a dead lift (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.17">v. 17</reference>): "When I had almost <hi type="italic">dwelt in silence,</hi> then the Lord was <hi type="italic">my help,</hi> kept me alive, kept me in heart; and <hi type="italic">unless I had</hi> made him <hi type="italic">my help,</hi> by putting my trust in him and expecting relief from him, I could never have kept possession of my own soul; but living by faith in him has kept my head above water, has given me breath, and something to say." (2.) God's goodness is the great support of sinking spirits (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When I said, My foot slips</hi> into sin, into ruin, into despair, then <hi type="italic">thy mercy, O Lord! held me up,</hi> kept me from falling, and defeated the design of those who consulted to <hi type="italic">cast me down from my excellency,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.62.4">Ps. lxii. 4</reference>. We are beholden not only to God's power, but to his pity, for spiritual supports: <hi type="italic">Thy mercy,</hi> the gifts of thy mercy and my hope in thy mercy, <hi type="italic">held me up.</hi> God's right hand sustains his people when they look on their right hand and on their left and there is none to uphold; and we are then prepared for his gracious supports when we are sensible of our own weakness and inability to stand by our own strength, and come to God, to acknowledge it, and to tell him how <hi type="italic">our foot slips.</hi> (3.) Divine consolations are the effectual relief of troubled spirits (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In the multitude of my thoughts within me,</hi> which are noisy like a multitude, crowding and jostling one another like a multitude, and very unruly and ungovernable, in the multitude of my sorrowful, solicitous, timorous thoughts, <hi type="italic">thy comforts delight my soul;</hi> and they are never more delightful than when they come in so seasonably to silence my unquiet thoughts and keep my mind easy." The world's comforts give but little delight to the soul when it is hurried with melancholy thoughts; they are songs to a heavy heart. But God's comforts will reach the soul, and not the fancy only, and will bring with them that peace and that pleasure which the smiles of the world cannot give and which the frowns of the world cannot take away. <div eID="gen12191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12192" type="x-p"/> 5. God is, and will be, as a righteous Judge, the patron and protector of right and the punisher and avenger of wrong; this the psalmist had both the assurance of and the experience of. (1.) He will give redress to the injured (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.22">v. 22</reference>): "When none else will, nor can, nor dare, shelter me, <hi type="italic">the Lord is my defence,</hi> to preserve me from the evil of my troubles, from sinking under them and being ruined by them; and he is <hi type="italic">the rock of my refuge,</hi> in the clefts of which I may take shelter, and on the top of which I may set my feet, to be out of the reach of danger." God is his people's refuge, to whom they may flee, in whom they are safe and may be secure; he is the rock of their refuge, so strong, so firm, impregnable, immovable, as a rock: natural fastnesses sometimes exceed artificial fortifications. (2.) He will reckon with the injurious (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall render to them their own iniquity;</hi> he shall deal with them according to their deserts, and that very mischief which they did and designed against God's people shall be brought upon themselves: it follows, <hi type="italic">He shall cut them off in their wickedness.</hi> A man cannot be more miserable than his own wickedness will make him if God visit it upon him: it will cut him in the remembrance of it; it will cut him off in the recompence of it. This the psalm concludes with the triumphant assurance of: <hi type="italic">Yea, the Lord our God,</hi> who takes our part and owns us for his, <hi type="italic">shall cut them off</hi> from any fellowship with him, and so shall make them completely miserable and their pomp and power shall stand them in no stead.  <chapter eID="Ps.94"/> <div eID="gen12192" type="x-p"/>

entries.ce17f142e0c8a97fca206dd337de04fc45d4a1ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6593"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 94</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.94.1-Ps.94.23">Psa 94:1-23</reference>. The writer, appealing to God in view of the oppression of enemies, rebukes them for their wickedness and folly, and encourages himself, in the confidence that God will punish evildoers, and favor His people.</title> <div sID="gen10102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6593"/>1-2. God's revenge is His judicial infliction of righteous punishment.<div eID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">show thyself--</hi>(Compare Margin). <div eID="gen10103" type="x-p"/>
entries.430ff5cb2c2e038b9e430a256b2ed332dc55dc05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6595"/><div sID="gen10105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6595"/>3-4. In an earnest expostulation he expresses his desire that the insolent triumph of the wicked may be ended. <div eID="gen10105" type="x-p"/>
entries.e554e743122dec12f87c6f221c77d8d8857f7adf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6596"/><div sID="gen10106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6596"/><hi type="bold">5-6. thy people [and] thine heritage--</hi>are synonymous, the people being often called God's heritage. As justice to the weak is a sign of the best government, their oppression is a sign of the worst (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.18">De 10:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.2">Is 10:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10106" type="x-p"/>
entries.6dff06bdd9a2daf24d7bcd798eaea06c71d2ce8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6597"/><div sID="gen10107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6597"/>7. Their cruelty is only exceeded by their wicked and absurd presumption (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">59:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10107" type="x-p"/>
entries.79bdcbe8192f474d15a5c5c51bb39805b5470525: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6598"/><div sID="gen10108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6598"/><hi type="bold">8. ye brutish--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.73.22">Psa 73:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.6">92:6</reference>). <div eID="gen10108" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1388169424ff1d2d4e3a32a4c71831c43e0548f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6599"/><div sID="gen10109" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6599"/>9-11. The evidence of God's providential government is found in His creative power and omniscience, which also assure us that He can punish the wicked in regard to all their vain purposes. <div eID="gen10109" type="x-p"/>
entries.298607bfe7e9e3bd244d4a05e10a9a60fcfcddc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6600"/><div sID="gen10110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6600"/>12-13. On the other hand He favors though He chastens, the pious, and will teach and preserve them till the prosperous wicked are overthrown. <div eID="gen10110" type="x-p"/>
entries.d834470bde02a1882d1980f4ed91ac744a6cade8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6601"/><div sID="gen10111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6601"/>14-15. This results from His abiding love (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>), which is further evinced by His restoring order in His government, whose right administration will be approved by the good. <div eID="gen10111" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac5a71251c0c95d4a6a1f5382c06dda92c5ffe50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6602"/><div sID="gen10112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6602"/>16. These questions imply that none other than God will help (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.9">Psa 60:9</reference>), <div eID="gen10112" type="x-p"/>
entries.121f991bffcd0a17825b57c956912005944fa9ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6603"/><div sID="gen10113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6603"/>17-19. a fact fully confirmed by his past experience.<div eID="gen10113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelt in silence--</hi>as in the grave (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.17">Psa 31:17</reference>). <div eID="gen10114" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c85f2b67e591261ac9ced5fc9e49a53d1a32d30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6605"/><div sID="gen10116" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6605"/><hi type="bold">20. throne--</hi>power, rulers.<div eID="gen10116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquity [and] mischief--</hi>both denote evils done to others, as <reference osisRef="Ps.94.21">Psa 94:21</reference> explains. <div eID="gen10117" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba040fa73bc899e276b2b8bb08e780ff5c88474e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6606"/><div sID="gen10118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6606"/>22-23. Yet he is safe in God's care.<div eID="gen10118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defence--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.59.9">Psa 59:9</reference>).<div eID="gen10119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rock of ... refuge--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.9.9">Psa 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">18:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10120" type="x-p"/>

entries.1850684b04fa8330c54444a4c524342d4e2ee533: <div eID="gen21721" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21722" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21723" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21723" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21722" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21724" type="x-p"/> An appeal to God against oppressors, <reference osisRef="Psa.94.1-Psa.94.7">Psa 94:1-7</reference>. Expostulations with the workers of iniquity, <reference osisRef="Psa.94.8-Psa.94.11">Psa 94:8-11</reference>. God's merciful dealings with his followers, <reference osisRef="Psa.94.12-Psa.94.15">Psa 94:12-15</reference>; and their confidence in him, <reference osisRef="Psa.94.16-Psa.94.19">Psa 94:16-19</reference>. The punishment of the wicked foretold, <reference osisRef="Psa.94.20-Psa.94.23">Psa 94:20-23</reference>. <div eID="gen21724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21725" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title either in the Hebrew or Chaldee. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, have "A Psalm of David, for the fourth day of the week;" but this gives us no information on which we can rely. In three of Kennicott's MSS. it is written as a part of the preceding. It is probably a prayer of the captives in Babylon for deliverance; and was written by the descendants of Moses, to whom some of the preceding Psalms have been attributed. It contains a description of an iniquitous and oppressive government, such as that under which the Israelites lived in Babylon. <div eID="gen21725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21726" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21727" type="x-p"/> O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth - God is the author of retributive justice, as well as of mercy. This retributive justice is what we often term vengeance, but perhaps improperly; for vengeance with us signifies an excitement of angry passions, in order to gratify a vindictive spirit, which supposes itself to have received some real injury; whereas what is here referred to is that simple act of justice which gives to all their due.
entries.b1b1ea878b888d800027c37525fab312f8dcf98e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21728" type="x-p"/> Lift up thyself - Exert thy power. <div eID="gen21728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21729" type="x-p"/> Render a reward to the proud - To the Babylonians, who oppress and insult us.
entries.b11ca186b9a3ac8b17e4db0949cd2e083cb60505: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21730" type="x-p"/> How long shall the wicked triumph? - The wicked are often in prosperity; and this only shows us of how little worth riches are in the sight of God, when he bestows them on the most contemptible of mortals. But their time and prosperity have their bounds.
entries.371690f015c8ee0ed25f135a14c19b16b9e36cce: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21731" type="x-p"/> They utter and speak - יביאו yabbiu, their hearts get full of pride and insolence; and then, from the abundance of such vile hearts, the mouth speaks; and the speech is of hard things, threatening which they are determined to execute, boastings of their power, authority, etc.
entries.b58684e53c43083186836d39be9d393204989d1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21732" type="x-p"/> They break in pieces thy people - This was true af the Babylonians. Nehuchadnezzar slew many; carried the rest into captivity; ruined Jerusalem; overturned the temple; sacked, pillaged, and destroyed all the country.
entries.f8bf81ed90d84365463d01733da461b07f4938df: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21733" type="x-p"/> They slay the widow - Nebuchadnezzar carried on his wars with great cruelty. He carried fire and sword every where; spared neither age, sex, nor condition. The widow, the orphan, and the stranger, persons in the most desolate condition of life, were not distinguished from others by his ruthless sword.
entries.aafd48f071c0dc1ed6b5bb8ba395f63dfd122963: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21734" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall not see - This was either the language of infidelity or insult. Indeed, what could the Babylonians know of the true God? They might consider him as the God of a district or province, who knew nothing and did nothing out of his own territories.
entries.52f4e7be716fdc12950287deb8433c9f857554e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21735" type="x-p"/> Understand, ye brutish - These are the same expressions as in <reference osisRef="Psa.92.6">Psa 92:6</reference> (note), on which see the note.
entries.0632c07a905171d96a03c93e75afe9b8f68acc51: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21736" type="x-p"/> He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? - This is allowed to be an unanswerable mode of argumentation. Whatever is found of excellence in the creature, must be derived from the Creator, and exist in him in the plenitude of infinite excellence. God, says St. Jerome, is all eye, because he sees all; he is all hand, because he does all things; he is all foot, for he is every where present. The psalmist does not say, He that planted the ear, hath he not an ear? He that formed the eye, hath he not eyes? No; but, Shall he not hear? Shall he not see! And why does he say so? To prevent the error of humanizing God, of attributing members or corporeal parts to the infinite Spirit. See Calmet.
entries.6bba294ff6778a453ed0d4b386919f7446b55103: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21737" type="x-p"/> He that chastiseth the heathen, shall not he correct? - You, who are heathens, and heathens of the most abandoned kind. <div eID="gen21737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21738" type="x-p"/> He that teacheth man knowledge - We here supply shall not he know? But this is not acknowledged by the original, nor by any of the Versions. <div eID="gen21738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21739" type="x-p"/> Indeed it is not necessary; for either the words contain a simple proposition, "It is he who teacheth man knowledge," or this clause should be read in connection with <reference osisRef="Psa.94.11">Psa 94:11</reference> : "Jehovah, who teacheth man knowledge, knoweth the devices of man, that they are vanity." As he teaches knowledge to man, must he not know all the reasonings and devices of the human heart?
entries.96b903a1aa3164349bd78c6189cc82c677b680aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21740" type="x-p"/> Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest - תיסרנו teyasserennu, whom thou instructest; and teachest him out of thy law. Two points here are worthy of our most serious regard: <div eID="gen21740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21741" type="x-p"/> 1. God gives knowledge to man: gives him understanding and reason. <div eID="gen21741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21742" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives him a revelation of himself; he places before that reason and understanding his Divine law. <div eID="gen21742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21743" type="x-p"/> This is God's system of teaching; and the human intellect is his gift, which enables man to understand this teaching. We perhaps may add a third thing here; that as by sin the understanding is darkened, he gives the Holy Spirit to dispel this darkness from the intellect, in order that his word may be properly apprehended and understood. But he gives no new faculty; he removes the impediments from the old, and invigorates it by his Divine energy.
entries.494776fd1ebfb7e0c7089c73a14239b0045b1965: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21744" type="x-p"/> That thou mayest give him rest - He whom God instructs is made wise unto salvation; and he who is thus taught has rest in his soul, and peace and confidence in adversity.
entries.f69104bceeaa832853021bde09eabe0eed956db2: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21745" type="x-p"/> The Lord will not cast off his people - Though they are now suffering under a grievous and oppressive captivity, yet the Lord hath not utterly cast them off. They are his inheritance, and he will again restore them to their own land.
entries.2208169d90f6e25184ce6c9834bd8d804dd6aa46: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21746" type="x-p"/> But judgment shall return unto righteousness - If we read יושב yosheb, shalt sit, for ישוב yashub, shall return, which is only placing the ו vau before the ש shin instead of after it, we have the following sense: Until the just one shall sit in judgment, and after him all the upright in heart. Cyrus has the epithet צדק tsedek, the just one, in different places in the Prophet Isaiah. See <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.10">Isa 41:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.5">Isa 51:5</reference>. It was Cyrus who gave liberty to the Jews, who appeared as their deliverer and conductor to their own land, and they are all represented as following in his train.
entries.3199f56dc1230177d7cc89de035341dbd42ca1d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21747" type="x-p"/> Who will rise up for me - Who is he that shall be the deliverer of thy people? Who will come to our assistance against these wicked Babylonians?
entries.483ea198405260f036a1985a48d25ecbd91c71c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21748" type="x-p"/> Unless the Lord had been my help - Had not God in a strange manner supported us while under his chastising hand, we had been utterly cut off. <div eID="gen21748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21749" type="x-p"/> My soul had almost dwelt in silence - The Vulgate has in inferno, in hell or the infernal world; the Septuagint, τῳ ᾁδῃ, in the invisible world.
entries.dc9de3f812a64b9189fac07a57514d172f6476f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen21749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21750" type="x-p"/> When I said, My foot slippeth - When I found myself so weak and my enemy so strong, that I got first off my guard, and then off my center of gravity, and my fall appeared inevitable: - <div eID="gen21750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21751" type="x-p"/> Thy mercy, O Lord, held me up - יסעדני yisadeni, propped me. It is a metaphor taken from any thing falling, that is propped, shored up, or buttressed. How often does the mercy of God thus prevent the ruin of weak believers, and of those who have been unfaithful!
entries.5bb0062aa92038630b1f04f7cee9ff3815aed900: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen21751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21752" type="x-p"/> In the multitude of my thoughts - Of my griefs, (dolorum, Vulgate); my sorrows, (οδυνων, Septuagint). According to the multitude of my trials and distresses, have been the consolations which thou hast afforded me. Or, While I have been deeply meditating on thy wondrous grace and mercy, Divine light has broken in upon my soul, and I have been filled with delight.
entries.acdbf539a26bf3411182bec7ac2a0f0d080fe884: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen21752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21753" type="x-p"/> Shall the throne of iniquity - No wicked king, judge, or magistrate shall ever stand in thy presence. No countenance shall such have from thy grace or providence. <div eID="gen21753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21754" type="x-p"/> Which frameth mischief - Devise, plan, and execute, as if they acted by a positive law, and were strictly enjoined to do what they so much delighted in.
entries.b883ebbd8594145197a7255b1e5fbc28af7c5233: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen21754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21755" type="x-p"/> They gather themselves together - In every thing that is evil, they are in unity. The devil, his angels, and his children, all join and draw together when they have for their object the destruction of the works of the Lord. But this was particularly the case with respect to the poor Jews among the Babylonians: they were objects of their continual hatred, and they labored for their destruction. <div eID="gen21755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21756" type="x-p"/> This and the following verses have been applied to our Lord, and the treatment he met with both from his own countrymen and from the Romans. They pretended to "judge him according to the law, and framed mischief against him;" they "assembled together against the life of the righteous one," and "condemned innocent blood;" but God evidently interposed, and "brought upon them their own iniquity," according to their horrible imprecation: "His blood be upon us and upon our children!" God "cut them off in their own iniquity." All this had, in reference to him, a most literal fulfillment.
entries.f61bf20f4343565c812cc1c457b62caf53ea2f35: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen21756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21757" type="x-p"/> The rock of my refuge - Alluding to those natural fortifications among rocks, which are frequent in the land of Judea.
entries.d4be8ea687e9f35844f4295f04a0bf9be7f60197: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen21757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21758" type="x-p"/> Shall cut them off - This is repeated, to show that the destruction of the Babylonians was fixed and indubitable: and in reference to the Jews, the persecutors and murderers of our Lord and his apostles, it was not less so. Babylon is totally destroyed; not even a vestige of it remains. The Jews are no longer a nation; they are scattered throughout the world, and have no certain place of abode. They do not possess even one village on the face of the earth. <div eID="gen21758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21759" type="x-p"/> The last verse is thus translated and paraphrased in the old Psalter: - <div eID="gen21759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21760" type="x-p"/> Trans. And he sal yelde to thaim thair wickednes, and in thair malice he sall skater thaim: skater thaim sal Lorde oure God. <div eID="gen21760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21761" type="x-p"/> Par - Alswa say efter thair il entent, that thai wil do gude men harme; he sall yelde thaim pyne, and in thair malice thai sal be sundred fra the hali courte of hevene, and skatred emang the wiked fendes of hell. <div eID="gen21761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21762" type="x-p"/> For different views of several parts of this Psalm, see the Analysis.  <chapter eID="Ps.94"/> <div eID="gen21762" type="x-p"/>

entries.bb5ddb3c0dec70861c41de6425f58be9f22651a3: <div eID="gen9928" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Consolation of Prayer under the Oppression of Tyrants</title> <div sID="gen9929" type="x-p"/> This Psalm, akin to <reference osisRef="Ps.92.1-Ps.92.15">Psa 92:1-15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5">Psa 93:1-5</reference> by the community of the anadiplosis, bears the inscription Ψαλμὸς ᾠδῆς τῷ Δαυίδ, τετράδι σαββάτου in the lxx. It is also a Talmudic tradition<note placement="foot">According to <hi type="italic">B. Erachin</hi> 11 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, at the time of the Chaldaean destruction of Jerusalem the Levites on their pulpits were singing this 94th Psalm, and as they came to the words “and He turneth back upon them their iniquity” (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.23">Psa 94:23</reference>), the enemies pressed into the Temple, so that they were not able to sing the closing words, “Jahve, our God, will destroy them.” To the scruple that Ps 94 is a Wednesday, not a Sunday, Psalm (that fatal day, however, was a Sunday, מוצאי שׁבת), it is replied, it may have been a lamentation song that had just been put into their mouths by the circumstances of that time (אלייא בעלמא דעלמא דנפל להו בפומייהו).</note> that it was the Wednesday song in the Temple liturgy (τετράδι σαββάτου = ברביעי בשׁבת). Athanasius explains it by a reference to the fourth month (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.2">Jer 39:2</reference>). The τῳ Δαυίδ, however, is worthless. It is a post-Davidic Psalm; for, although it comes out of one mould, we still meet throughout with reminiscences of older Davidic and Asaphic models. The enemies against whom it supplicates the appearing of the God of righteous retribution are, as follows from a comparison of <reference osisRef="Ps.94.5">Psa 94:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.8">Psa 94:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.10">Psa 94:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Psa 94:12</reference>, non-Israelites, who despise the God of Israel and fear not His vengeance, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">Psa 94:7</reference>; whose barbarous doings, however, call forth, even among the oppressed people themselves, foolish doubts concerning Jahve’s omniscient beholding and judicial interposition. Accordingly the Psalm is one of the latest, but not necessarily a Maccabaean Psalm. The later Persian age, in which the Book of Ecclesiastes was written, could also exhibit circumstances and moods such as these.
entries.061fa8e83e2339bd4339147e93a44d0789ecd033: <reference osisRef="Ps.94.1-Ps.94.3">Psa 94:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> The first strophe prays that God would at length put a judicial restraint upon the arrogance of ungodliness. Instead of חופיע (a less frequent form of the imperative for הופע, Ges. §53, rem. 3) it was perhaps originally written הופיעה (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Psa 80:2</reference>), the <hi type="italic">He</hi> of which has been lost owing to the <hi type="italic">He</hi> that follows. The plural נקמות signifies not merely single instances of taking vengeance (<reference osisRef="Ezek.25.17">Eze 25:17</reference>, cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.48">Psa 18:48</reference>), but also intensively complete revenge or recompense (Jdg 11:36; <reference osisRef="2Sam.4.8">2Sa 4:8</reference>). The designation of God is similar to אל גּמלות in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.56">Jer 51:56</reference>, and the anadiplosis is like <reference osisRef="Ps.94.3">Psa 94:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.23">Psa 94:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>, Psa 93:3. הנּשׂא, lift Thyself up, arise, viz., in judicial majesty, calls to mind Psa 7:7. השׁיב גּמוּל is construed with על (cf. ל, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">Psa 28:4</reference>; 59:18) as in Joe 3:4. With גּאים accidentally accord ἀγαυός and κύδεΐ γαίων in the epic poets.
entries.166132b3d22ab4615c04a80c68d55517b345348f: <reference osisRef="Ps.94.4-Ps.94.7">Psa 94:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> The second strophe describes those over whom the first prays that the judgment of God may come. הבּיע (cf. הטּיף) is a tropical phrase used of that kind of speech that results from strong inward impulse and flows forth in rich abundance. The poet himself explains how it is here (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.59.8">Psa 59:8</reference>) intended: they speak עתק, that which is unrestrained, unbridled, insolent (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Psa 31:19</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. התאמּר Schultens interprets <hi type="italic">ut Emiri</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">'mı̂r</hi>, a commander) <hi type="italic">se gerunt</hi>; but אמיר signifies in Hebrew the top of a tree (vid., on <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9">Isa 17:9</reference>); and from the primary signification to tower aloft, whence too אמר, to speak, prop. <hi type="italic">effere = effari</hi>, התאמּר, like התימּר in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">Isa 61:6</reference>, directly signifies to exalt one’s self, to carry one’s self high, to strut. On ודכּאוּ cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.22">Pro 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.15">Isa 3:15</reference>; and on their atheistical principle which ויּאמרוּ places in closest connection with their mode of action, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.8">Psa 59:8</reference> <hi type="italic">extrem</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in יּהּ, distinct from the <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. in the same word in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Psa 94:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">Psa 118:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.18">Psa 118:18</reference>, is the <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conjunct. </hi>according to the rule of the so-called דחיק.
entries.da947e855e2d43bd9af204ebf16c727e729db9a6: <reference osisRef="Ps.94.8-Ps.94.11">Psa 94:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> The third strophe now turns from those bloodthirsty, blasphemous oppressors of the people of God whose conduct calls forth the vengeance of Jahve, to those among the people themselves, who have been puzzled about the omniscience and indirectly about the righteousness of God by the fact that this vengeance is delayed. They are called בערים and כסילים in the sense of Psa 73:21. Those hitherto described against whom God’s vengeance is supplicated are this also; but this appellation would be too one-sided for them, and בּעם refers the address expressly to a class of men among the people whom those oppress and slay. It is absurd that God, the planter of the ear (הנּטע, like שׁסע in <reference osisRef="Lev.11.7">Lev 11:7</reference>, with an accented <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>, because the <hi type="italic">praet. Kal</hi> does not follow the rule for the drawing back of the accent called נסוג אחור) and the former of the eye (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.4.11">Exo 4:11</reference>), should not be able to hear and to see; everything that is excellent in the creature, God must indeed possess in original, absolute perfection.<note placement="foot">The questions are not: ought He to have no ear, etc.; as Jerome pertinently observes in opposition to the anthropomorphites, <hi type="italic">membra tulit, efficientias dedit</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9933" type="x-p"/> The poet then points to the extra-Israelitish world and calls God יסר גּוים, which cannot be made to refer to a warning by means of the voice of conscience; יסר used thus without any closer definition does not signify “warning,” but “chastening” (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.7">Pro 9:7</reference>). Taking his stand upon facts like those in <reference osisRef="Job.12.23">Job 12:23</reference>, the poet assumes the punitive judicial rule of God among the heathen to be an undeniable fact, and presents for consideration the question, whether He who chasteneth nations cannot and will not also punish the oppressors of His church (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.18.25">Gen 18:25</reference>), He who teacheth men knowledge, i.e., He who nevertheless must be the omnipotent One, since all knowledge comes originally from Him? Jahve - thus does the course of argument close in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">Psa 94:11</reference> - sees through (ידע of penetrative perceiving or knowing that goes to the very root of a matter) the thoughts of men that they are vanity. Thus it is to be interpreted, and not: for they (men) are vanity; for this ought to have been כּי הבל המּה, whereas in the dependent clause, when the predicate is not intended to be rendered especially prominent, as in Ps 9:21, the pronominal subject may precede, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.9">Isa 61:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.5">Jer 46:5</reference> (Hitzig). The rendering of the lxx (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.20">1Co 3:20</reference>), ὅτι εἰσὶ μάταιοι (Jerome, <hi type="italic">quoniam vanae sunt</hi>), is therefore correct; המּה, with the customary want of exactness, stands for הנּה. It is true men themselves are הבל; it is not, however, on this account that He who sees through all things sees through their thoughts, but He sees through them in their sinful vanity.
entries.545c67e087d0a99c5793fb8c04364d0e4af86205: <reference osisRef="Ps.94.12-Ps.94.15">Psa 94:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen9933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9934" type="x-p"/> The fourth strophe praises the pious sufferer, whose good cause God will at length aid in obtaining its right. The “blessed” reminds one of <reference osisRef="Ps.34.9">Psa 34:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">Psa 40:5</reference>, and more especially of <reference osisRef="Job.5.17">Job 5:17</reference>, cf. Pro 3:11. Here what are meant are sufferings like those bewailed in Psa 94:5., which are however, after all, the well-meant dispensations of God. Concerning the aim and fruit of purifying and testing afflictions God teaches the sufferer out of His Law (cf. e.g., Deu 8:5.), in order to procure him rest, viz., inward rest (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">Jer 49:23</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.30.15">Isa 30:15</reference>), i.e., not to suffer him to be disheartened and tempted by days of wickedness, i.e., wicked, calamitous days (Ew. §287, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), until (and it will inevitably come to pass) the pit is finished being dug into which the ungodly falls headlong (cf. Psa 112:7.). יּהּ has the emphatic <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, which properly does not double, and still less unite, but requires an emphatic pronunciation of the letter, which might easily become inaudible. The initial <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> of the divine name might easily lose it consonantal value here in connection with the preceding toneless <hi type="italic">û</hi>,<note placement="foot">If it is correct that, as Aben-Ezra and Parchon testify, the וּ, as being compounded of <hi type="italic">o</hi> (<hi type="italic">u</hi>) + <hi type="italic">i</hi>, was pronounced <hi type="italic">ü</hi> like the <hi type="italic">u</hi> in the French word <hi type="italic">pur</hi> by the inhabitants of Palestine, then this <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, in accordance with its orthophonic function, is the more intelligible in cases like תיסרנו יּה and קראתי יּה, cf. Pinsker, <hi type="italic">Einleitung</hi>, S. 153, and Geiger, <hi type="italic">Urschrift</hi>, S. 277. In קומו צּאו, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.14">Gen 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.31">Exo 12:31</reference>, קומו סּעו, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.24">Deu 2:24</reference>, <hi type="italic">Tsade</hi> and <hi type="italic">Samech</hi> have this <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> for the same reason as the <hi type="italic">Sin</hi> in תשׁביתו שּׁאור, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.15">Exo 12:15</reference> (vid., Heidenheim on that passage), viz., because there is a danger in all these cases of slurring over the sharp sibilant. Even Chajug' (vid., Ewald and Dukes’ <hi type="italic">Beiträge</hi>, iii. 23) confuses this <hi type="italic">Dag. orthophonicum</hi> with the <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conjunctivum</hi>.</note> and the <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. guards against this: cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">Psa 118:5</reference>, Psa 118:18. The certainty of the issue that is set in prospect by עד is then confirmed with כּי. It is impossible that God can desert His church - He cannot do this, because in general right must finally come to His right, or, as it is here expressed, משׁפּט must turn to צדק, i.e., the right that is now subdued must at length be again strictly maintained and justly administered, and “after it then all who are upright in heart,” i.e., all such will side with it, joyously greeting that which has been long missed and yearned after. משׁפּט is fundamental right, which is at all times consistent with itself and raised above the casual circumstances of the time, and צדק, like אמת in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.3">Isa 42:3</reference>, is righteousness (justice), which converts this right into a practical truth and reality.
entries.aba3b0e483370b8ca7ec8e22cf51a64d91cf9fa8: <reference osisRef="Ps.94.16-Ps.94.19">Psa 94:16-19</reference> <div eID="gen9934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9935" type="x-p"/> In the fifth strophe the poet celebrates the praise of the Lord as his sole, but also trusty and most consolatory help. The meaning of the question in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">Psa 94:16</reference> is, that there is no man who would rise and succour him in the conflict with the evil-doers; ל as in <reference osisRef="Exod.14.25">Exo 14:25</reference>; Jdg 6:31, and עם (without נלחם or the like) in the sense of <hi type="italic">contra</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>, cf. 2Ch 20:6. God alone is his help. He alone has rescued him from death. היה is to be supplied to לוּלי: if He had not been, or: if He were not; and the apodosis is: then very little would have been wanting, then it would soon have come to this, that his soul would have taken up its abode, etc.; cf. on the construction <reference osisRef="Ps.119.92">Psa 119:92</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.5">Psa 124:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.9">Isa 1:9</reference>, and on כּמעט with the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. <reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Psa 73:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.87">Psa 119:87</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.26.10">Gen 26:10</reference> (on the other hand with the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <reference osisRef="Ps.81.15">Psa 81:15</reference>). דּוּמה is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.17">Psa 115:17</reference>, the silence of the grave and of Hades; here it is the object to שׁכנה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">Psa 37:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.12">Pro 8:12</reference>, and frequently. When he appears to himself already as one that has fallen, God’s mercy holds him up. And when thoughts, viz., sad and fearful thoughts, are multiplied within him, God’s comforts delight him, viz., the encouragement of His word and the inward utterances of His Spirit. שׁרעפּים, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.23">Psa 139:23</reference>, is equivalent to שעפּים, from שׂעף, סעף, Arab. <hi type="italic">š‛b</hi>, to split, branch off (<hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 181; tr. p. 214). The plural form ישׁעשׁעוּ, like the plural of the imperative in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Isa 29:9</reference>, has two <hi type="italic">Pathachs</hi>, the second of which is the “independentification” of the <hi type="italic">Chateph</hi> of ישׁעשׁע.
entries.2349e457cd887391d2b5dd933a7f2cf50117b8f1: <reference osisRef="Ps.94.20-Ps.94.23">Psa 94:20-23</reference> <div eID="gen9935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9936" type="x-p"/> In the sixth strophe the poet confidently expects the inevitable divine retribution for which he has earnestly prayed in the introduction. יחברך is erroneously accounted by many (and by Gesenius too) as <hi type="italic">fut. Pual</hi> = יחבּרך = יחבּר עמּך, a vocal contraction together with a giving up of the reduplication in favour of which no example can be advanced. It is <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> = יחברך, from יחבּר = יחבּר, with the same regression of the modification of the vowel<note placement="foot">By means of a similar transposition of the vowel as is to be assumed in תּאהבוּ, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.22">Pro 1:22</reference>, it also appears that מדוּבּין = מוּסבּין (lying upon the table, ἀνακείμενοι) of the Pesach-Haggada has to be explained, which Joseph Kimchi finds so inexplicable that he regards it as a clerical error that has become traditional.</note> as in יחנך = יחנך in <reference osisRef="Gen.43.29">Gen 43:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.19">Isa 30:19</reference> (Hupfeld), but as in verbs <hi type="italic">primae gutturalis</hi>, so also in כּתבם, כּתבם, inflected from כּתב, Ew. §251, <hi type="italic">d</hi>. It might be more readily regarded as <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> than as <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> (like תּאכלנוּ, <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">Job 20:26</reference>), but the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> too already signifies to enter into fellowship (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.3">Gen 14:3</reference>; Hos 4:17), therefore (similarly to יגרך, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.5">Psa 5:5</reference>) it is<hi type="italic">: num consociabitur tecum</hi>. כּסּא is here the judgment-seat, just as the Arabic <hi type="italic">cursi</hi> directly denotes the tribunal of God (in distinction from Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛arš</hi>, the throne of His majesty). With reference to הוּות vid., on Psa 5:10. Assuming that חק is a divine statute, we obtain this meaning for עלי־חק: which frameth (i.e., plots and executes) trouble, by making the written divine right into a rightful title for unrighteous conduct, by means of which the innocent are plunged into misfortune. Hitzig renders: contrary to order, after <reference osisRef="Prov.17.26">Pro 17:26</reference>, where, however, על־ישׁר is intended like ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης, Mat 5:10. Olshausen proposes to read יגוּרוּ (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.7">Psa 56:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">Psa 59:4</reference>) instead of יגודּוּ, just as conversely Aben-Ezra in <reference osisRef="Ps.56.7">Psa 56:7</reference> reads יגודּוּ. But גּדד, גּוּד, has the secured signification of <hi type="italic">scindere, incidere</hi> (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">jdd</hi>, but also <hi type="italic">chd</hi>, <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 255), from which the signification <hi type="italic">invadere</hi> can be easily derived (whence גּדוּד, a breaking in, invasion, an invading host). With reference to דּם נקי vid., <hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 243 (tr. p. 286): because the blood is the soul, that is said of the blood which applies properly to the person. The subject to יגודו are the seat of corruption (by which a high council consisting of many may be meant, just as much as a princely throne) and its accomplices. Prophetic certainty is expressed in ויהי and ויּשׁב. The figure of God as משׂגּב is Davidic and Korahitic. צוּר מחסּי צוּר is explained from Psa 18:2. Since השׁיב designates the retribution as a return of guilt incurred in the form of actual punishment, it might be rendered “requite” just as well as “cause to return;” עליהם, however, instead of להם (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">Psa 54:7</reference>) makes the idea expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference> more natural. On ברעתם Hitzig correctly compares <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.7">2Sa 14:7</reference>; 2Sa 3:27. The Psalm closes with an anadiplosis, just as it began with one; and אלהינוּ affirms that the destruction of the persecutor will follow as surely as the church is able to call Jahve its God.  <chapter eID="Ps.94"/> <div eID="gen9936" type="x-p"/>

entries.afdb498caac30d8c5c5f2532cf4935f18c1c1dc8:
PSALM 94
The Psalmist implores Divine assistance against wicked and violent men, who persecuted the upright in a cruel and tyrannical manner. It is evident that he refers to domestic foes, whose unrighteous domination was as vexatious and oppressive to the Lord’s people, as all the injuries received from the Gentile nations without.
Psalm 94:1-6
1. O Jehovah! God of vengeances; God of vengeances,
This is a literal translation of the original Hebrew, and Archbishop Secker thinks it is much more spirited than that of our English version. The word vengeance, when applied to God, means nothing more than his retributive justice. It may not be one of the happiest words for representing the Hebrew term when used to express this attribute of Deity, being liable to be misunderstood, as if it implied a revengeful spirit, the sense which it commonly bears when applied to men. “This retributive justice,” says Dr Adam Clarke, “is what we often term vengeance, but perhaps improperly; for vengeance with us signifies an excitement of angry passions, in order to gratify a vindictive spirit, which supposes itself to have received some real injury; whereas, what is here referred to is the simple act of justice that gives to all their due.”
shine forth.
Mant renders,
“Beam forth with all thy radiance bright.”
“The Hebrew verb,” he observes, “signifies to irradiate, shine forth, as God in glory; Psalm 80:1; 50:2; and that either in vengeance, as in this place, or kindness, as in Job 10:3.” — See Parkhurst’s Lexicon on יפע
2. Lift up thyself, thou Judge of the earth! render a reward to the proud. 3. O Jehovah! how long shall the wicked — how long shall the wicked triumph? 4. They pour forth, they speak hard things, all the workers of iniquity lift up themselves. 5. They break in pieces thy people, O Jehovah! and afflict thy inheritance. 6. They slay the widow, and the stranger, and murder the fatherless.
 
1 O Jehovah! God of vengeances We know that the Jews were surrounded by many neighbors who were not well affected towards them, and were thus incessantly subject to the assaults and oppression of bitter enemies. As this intestine persecution was even more afflictive than the rampant and unrestrained violence of the wicked, we need not wonder that the Psalmist should earnestly beseech God for deliverance from it. The expressions which he uses, calling upon God to shine forth conspicuously, and lift himself up on high, amount in common language to this, that God would give some actual manifestation of his character as judge or avenger; for in that case he is seen ascending his tribunal to exact the punishment due to sin, and demonstrate his power in preserving order and government in the world. The phraseology is used only in reference to ourselves, disposed as we are to feel as if he overlooked us, unless he stretched out his hand to help us in some visible and open manner. In calling him twice successively the God of vengeances, and then, judge of the earth, the Psalmist uses these titles as applicable to the present situation in which he stood, reminding Him in a manner of the office which belonged to him, and saying — O Lord! it is thine to take vengeance upon sinners, and judge the earth — see how they take advantage of the impunity which is extended to their guilt, and triumph audaciously in their wickedness! Not that God needs to be admonished of his duty, for he never resigns himself to indifference, and even when he seems to delay his judgments, is only adjusting them according to what he knows to be the best season; but his people conceive of him in this way to themselves, and take occasion from this to embolden and stimulate themselves to greater vehemency in prayer.
“Mais les fideles s’arrestent a mediter ainsi en eux-mesmes la nature d’iceluy, afin de s’accourager, meilleure esperance, et soliciter a prier avec plus grande ardeur et vehemence.” — Fr.
The same may be said of the repetition which the Psalmist uses. When the wicked then indulge in unrestrained excesses, we are to remember that God can never cease to assert his character as the judge of the earth who takes vengeance upon iniquity. Does he seem in our carnal apprehension to have at any time withdrawn and hidden himself? let us put up without hesitation the prayer which is here taught us by the Holy Spirit, that he would shine forth
